reference.source: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery / Sabiston Textbook of Surgery
clinicalPearls: Presents with acute, constant, throbbing perianal or rectal pain, often with a tender fluctuant swelling, fever, and malaise
Classified by anatomical space into perianal, ischiorectal, intersphincteric, and supralevator abscesses, each with characteristic examination findings
Most arise from infection of the anal glands opening into the crypts at the dentate line (the cryptoglandular theory)
A superficial perianal abscess is visibly red and fluctuant, whereas a deeper ischiorectal or supralevator abscess may cause deep pain and systemic upset with little external sign
Treatment is prompt surgical incision and drainage; antibiotics alone are inadequate and delay is dangerous
A significant proportion of drained abscesses are associated with, or later develop, a fistula-in-ano
Diabetes, immunosuppression, and Crohn's disease predispose to abscess formation and to more aggressive, spreading infection
Spreading perianal sepsis with systemic toxicity may herald necrotising infection (Fournier's gangrene), which is a surgical emergency
reference.pathophysiology: Anorectal abscesses usually begin with obstruction and infection of an anal gland at the base of an anal crypt (cryptoglandular infection). Pus tracks along planes of least resistance from the intersphincteric space into the perianal, ischiorectal, or supralevator spaces, and can extend circumferentially in a horseshoe pattern. The causative organisms are typically gut flora, including coliforms and anaerobes. Underlying conditions such as Crohn's disease, diabetes, and immunosuppression predispose to formation and to more extensive spread. Persistence of the primary gland infection after drainage creates the epithelialised track of a fistula-in-ano.
additionalDifferentials: Anal or rectal malignancy with sepsis
additionalInvestigations: Clinical examination and, where pain permits, digital rectal examination to assess deeper spaces
Examination under anaesthesia to fully assess and drain the collection and look for a fistula
MRI pelvis or endoanal ultrasound for complex, recurrent, or supralevator disease
Blood glucose and screening for immunosuppression, and blood cultures if systemically septic
Consideration of investigations for Crohn's disease in recurrent or atypical abscesses
redFlags: Spreading cellulitis, crepitus, skin necrosis, or disproportionate pain suggesting Fournier's gangrene (surgical emergency)
Systemic sepsis with tachycardia, hypotension, or confusion
Immunocompromise or poorly controlled diabetes with rapid progression
Deep or supralevator sepsis with minimal external signs but severe pain and toxicity
reference.prognosis: Simple abscesses drained promptly resolve well, but recurrence and fistula formation are common. Delayed treatment, deep spaces, immunosuppression, or necrotising infection markedly worsen outcomes and can be life-threatening.
pitfalls: Relying on antibiotics instead of prompt incision and drainage
Missing a deep ischiorectal or supralevator abscess because external signs are minimal
Failing to recognise early Fournier's gangrene in a diabetic or immunosuppressed patient
Overzealous probing for a fistula at the time of acute drainage, risking a false track
references: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
management: Perform prompt surgical incision and drainage as the definitive treatment, since antibiotics alone are inadequate and delay is dangerous
Add antibiotics targeting gut coliforms and anaerobes only for surrounding cellulitis, systemic sepsis, immunosuppression, diabetes, or valvular risk
Resuscitate with fluids and provide analgesia where there is systemic upset
Undertake examination under anaesthesia to assess deep ischiorectal or supralevator spaces and identify a coexisting fistula
Manage the drained cavity with open wound care and follow up for later development of a fistula-in-ano
Identify and treat predisposing conditions including diabetes, Crohn's disease, and immunosuppression
Escalate urgently for necrotising perineal infection with aggressive debridement and broad-spectrum antimicrobials
